LYON — The city council voted on Tuesday to extend the late-night tram service on three of its busiest lines, a decision that transport officials said would cost roughly 2.4 million euros a year and serve an estimated 9,000 additional riders each weekend.

The extension, which takes effect in January, follows a year-long pilot on the number 4 line that drew more passengers than planners had projected. Ridership on the pilot route rose by 31 percent between midnight and two in the morning, according to figures released by the regional transport authority last month.

"We were frankly surprised by the demand," said Claire Morel, the authority's head of service planning, in an interview after the vote. "People were already making these trips. They were just doing it by taxi, or they were walking home in the cold."

Not everyone on the council was persuaded. Several members of the opposition argued that the money would be better spent on daytime frequency in the suburbs, where buses on some routes run only every 20 minutes outside rush hour. One councillor described the extension as a subsidy for nightlife in the city centre.

Supporters countered that the late service mainly benefits shift workers, including hospital staff and hospitality employees whose working hours end after the regular network closes. A survey conducted during the pilot found that just over half of late-night riders were travelling to or from work.

The transport authority said it would publish a full evaluation of the extended service after its first twelve months, and that further expansion would depend on whether ridership on the new lines matches the results of the pilot.
